claims.text: The starting material is a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state.
The starting material is produced by a conventional route such as casting.
Controlled additive manufacturing followed by post-build heat treatment will refine the alloy microstructure relative to conventional casting.
Additive manufacturing produces rapid solidification and repeated thermal cycling.
Rapid solidification and repeated thermal cycling promote grain refinement in this alloy.
The AM intervention will create a refined sub-grain microstructure with enhanced grain-boundary characteristics.
The AM intervention may form nanoscale precipitates because of rapid solidification and repeated thermal cycling.
AM-induced sub-grain boundaries and minor dispersoids will stabilize the single-phase structure.
AM-induced sub-grain boundaries and minor dispersoids will impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion will improve the alloy's high-temperature mechanical properties.
The AM-processed alloy will have higher elevated-temperature yield strength than the same composition produced by conventional casting.
The AM-processed alloy will have better elevated-temperature creep resistance than the same composition produced by conventional casting.
The predicted improvement applies at approximately 600°C to 800°C.
The hypothesis applies when titanium and nickel are primary constituents of the high-entropy alloy rather than minor additions.

contradictions.description: The alloy is framed as a single-phase solid solution and the mechanism claims stabilization of that single-phase structure, while also predicting nanoscale precipitates or dispersoids. Such second-phase features would ordinarily make the resulting microstructure multiphase unless they are instead solute clusters or another feature not constituting a distinct phase.
